title: Run a small read on the isolate that asked for it
impact: Moonshot, rejected — but it priced the number four earlier experiments argued against without measuring. Exps 258, 264 and 239 each closed a candidate against a `select() round-trip floor`; on the canonical 6-column point read that floor is 6.3 us of an 8.4 us read, so anything rejected as below it was compared against a denominator four times larger than the work it competed with. Measured by running the query on the calling isolate when the per-SQL row-count high-water mark exps 260/264 keep says it has never returned more than 64 rows: a reproduced -74.8% on that point read, -71.0% at 21 columns (flat in projection width, unlike exp 264, because what is removed is per-request), -35.7% on a 20-row page, and -94.9% for a point read issued while four 1,000-row reads hold the whole pool — admission cost, the half every prior transfer measurement in this direction held constant. The guard lane written to kill it inverted: eight concurrent point reads are 70% faster run serially inline than four-wide across the pool, because parallelism cannot recover a per-request overhead larger than the request. Rejected anyway, and for a reason none of the numbers show. Every kill condition tested whether the row-count hint was *wrong*, which is the one failure mode the abort-and-fall-back row cap already handles; none tested whether row count is the right thing to predict from. It is not, along three independent axes: one row can be a 5 MB image (`SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` keeps a permanent high-water mark of 1, and with no hop to serialise for, exp 236's blob wrap is suppressed, so it copies unchecked onto the calling isolate); `count(*)` and unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` return few rows after unbounded work that precedes the first row; and an inline read returns a `List` rather than a `Future`, so N of them drain in microtasks as one uninterruptible block instead of N interleavable slices. All nine lanes were small integers and short TEXT on a hot cache, so none could see any of it — a guard set derived from the lanes you already have tests the hypothesis you already believe. The transferable rule: a safety property must be enforced, not predicted. The row cap survives because it aborts mid-decode and is correct whether or not the hint was right; a successor needs byte and VM-step caps beside it — both available from SQLite mid-flight — plus an answer to microtask coalescing that neither provides. Harness kept as the routing gate with its three missing lanes named; prototype at `archive/exp-265`.
